title: An Anthropic researcher just gave us a peek at self-improving AI
content:
Training AI models with other AI models has become a very popular goal for neolabs — and now, a researcher in Anthropic’s fellows program has given us an early look at what it might look like in practice.
On Friday, Anthropic published a new paper titled “Automated Researchers Can Reliably Mitigate Alignment Failures,” detailing how AI systems could reliably improve a model’s performance on a set of alignment benchmarks. When given 10 benchmarks for specific misaligned behaviors, the automated systems were able to improve performance on every single one without degrading overall performance.
Led by Anthropic fellow Chen Yueh-Han, the system replicates much of the traditional approach to research. Each automated system searches the available literature, proposes a method, and trains the model using that method for 30 minutes, gradually increasing the benchmark over several iterations. Effective methods are preserved while ineffective ones are discarded, allowing the system to operate quickly and at a great scale.
“Overall, these results provide early evidence that automated alignment post-training could become practical in the near term,” the paper reads.
The paper is a step toward recursive self-improvement, which many see as the next significant step in AI progress. If models can improve their own alignment training, it’s plausible they could improve training practices more broadly — at which point, human AI researchers might soon become obsolete.
The paper isn’t shy about addressing this idea, explicitly comparing the Automated Alignment Researcher (AAR) to its human equivalent. “The best AAR method beats what experienced humans propose, on average within six hours,” the paper reads. “Human guided research directions do not lead to stronger performance.”
There’s even a cost comparison, in case anyone wasn’t convinced. “An AAR costs roughly $4 per hour in API inference against the $150 per hour we pay our human researchers.”
In fairness, the paper also points out a few limitations to this approach. The automated system only works insofar as the benchmarks reflect the actual alignment goals, and even then there’s significant work to be done in establishing and maintaining those benchmarks — not to mention maintaining and expanding on the literature the automated researchers are drawn from.

report.summary: Anthropic's new paper shows AI systems can improve alignment benchmarks on their own, hinting at recursive self-improvement and cheaper automated research.
report.background: Training AI models with other AI models is a growing focus for frontier labs, and recursive self-improvement is often seen as AI's next major leap. Anthropic's fellows program, led by researcher Chen Yueh-Han, published a paper detailing an Automated Alignment Researcher (AAR) that improves a model's alignment behavior. Given 10 benchmarks for specific misaligned behaviors, the system improved performance on all of them without degrading overall performance. The AAR mimics human research by searching literature, proposing methods, and training for 30-minute iterations, keeping successful approaches and discarding failures. It can operate at scale quickly and cheaply, drawing comparisons to human researchers while also raising existential questions about the future role of human AI researchers.
key_points: Anthropic's paper, 'Automated Researchers Can Reliably Mitigate Alignment Failures,' describes an AI system that improves model alignment on all 10 tested benchmarks without hurting overall performance. This demonstrates a practical near-term method for automated alignment post-training.

The system works like a human researcher: it searches literature, proposes a method, trains the model for 30 minutes, then iterates. Effective methods are kept, ineffective ones dropped, allowing large-scale, rapid experimentation.

The best automated method beat what experienced human researchers proposed on average within six hours, according to the paper. The cost gap is stark too: about $4 per hour in API inference versus $150 per hour for human researchers.

The approach is a step toward recursive self-improvement, where AI improves its own training. However, its effectiveness depends heavily on benchmarks accurately reflecting alignment goals, and it requires ongoing maintenance of benchmarks and research literature.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this suggests alignment research could become much faster and cheaper, potentially accelerating safety work while also opening the door to recursive self-improvement. Developers might soon use automated researchers to polish model behavior instead of manually designing every training step, lowering costs for all. Regular users may see safer, more predictable AI products sooner. But there are risks: if AI systems improve themselves, human oversight becomes less central, and errors in benchmarks or literature could be amplified. The role of human researchers may shift from doing experiments to defining goals, maintaining benchmarks, and deciding when automated self-improvement is safe.
report.tools: Readers interested in following up can start with Anthropic's research page for the AAR paper. Open-source evaluation tools like EleutherAI's LM Evaluation Harness can help measure alignment metrics, while Anthropic's Constitutional AI framework offers insights into self-critique and training. For automated training pipelines, Hugging Face TRL and Axolotl provide flexible fine-tuning libraries that can be adapted for iterative, benchmark-driven methods like those described.
